title: Spotting and Beating Burnout
hook: Burnout isn't just being tired — it's exhaustion, cynicism, and feeling ineffective, and it comes from chronic stress you haven't been able to offload.
key_points: WHO ties burnout specifically to chronic, unmanaged workplace stress.
Three signs: exhaustion, cynicism or distance, and reduced effectiveness.
Recovery needs more than a weekend off — it needs real boundaries and rest.
Burnout is not a medical diagnosis, but it's a signal worth acting on.
content_html: "Burnout" gets used for any kind of tiredness, but it has a sharper meaning. The World Health Organization defines it precisely — as what happens when chronic stress at work goes unmanaged for too long — and naming it clearly is the first step to recovering from it.
extra_html: The WHO describes burnout as an occupational phenomenon — explicitly tied to the workplace, and explicitly not a medical diagnosis. It shows up across three dimensions: feeling drained and exhausted, growing mentally distant from or cynical about your job, and feeling less effective at it. Because the root cause is chronic stress that hasn't been offloaded, a single weekend off rarely fixes it; recovery usually means changing the conditions — setting real boundaries on hours and availability, protecting rest and recovery time, asking for support or workload changes, and reconnecting with parts of the work or life that feel meaningful. Burnout overlaps with conditions like depression, so if low mood, hopelessness, or trouble functioning persist, see a clinician — this isn't a substitute for medical advice.

related.title: What Stress Does to Your Body
related.hook: A jolt of stress is useful — it sharpens you for a real threat. The problem is when the alarm never switches off, and the body pays for staying on high alert.

related.title: Quick Ways to Calm Down
related.hook: When stress spikes, you can't think your way calm — but you can breathe your way there. A few simple tools work in minutes, anywhere.

related.title: Building Everyday Resilience
related.hook: Resilience isn't a personality you're born with — it's a set of habits and connections you can build, the way you build a muscle.

flashcards.prompt: How does the WHO define the three dimensions of burnout?

choices.text: Exhaustion, cynicism or distance from the job, and reduced effectiveness
Sadness, sleeplessness, and loss of appetite

flashcards.explanation_html: The WHO characterizes burnout by energy depletion or exhaustion, increased mental distance or cynicism toward one's job, and reduced professional efficacy.

flashcards.prompt: Per the WHO, what causes burnout — and is it a medical diagnosis?
flashcards.back_html: Burnout results from chronic workplace stress that hasn't been successfully managed. The WHO classifies it as an occupational phenomenon, not a medical condition or diagnosis.
